title: Can Gen Z be swayed by âFOMOâ, âMIAâ or âdeluluâ?
text: Hello and welcome to the 101st edition of The Weekly Vine. A hundred editions is a long time for one format, and now, to paraphrase the great American songwriter Robert Allen Zimmerman, itâs time for a little change. Instead of whining, sorry, Vining, about five different topics, we are going to focus on one topic and one topic only. People keep asking me what I think of the student protests . They probably wouldnât if they knew that when I was in Class I, I copied my motherâs signature in the school diary in protest against the authoritarian, Big Brotherly tendencies of teachers. Instead of acknowledging my right to privacy, the school almost expelled me. My only regret till now is that I wasnât proficient enough at cursive writing to get away with it. Anyway, back to the question: why do folks ask me what I think? Because they have been hoodwinked by the Macaulay-Higgins Complex , a term yours truly created that Googleâs AI mode confidently describes as the âpost-colonial tendency to treat people who speak and write English fluently as intellectually, socially and morally superiorâ. And perhaps people keep asking me what I think because I usually answer in Tharoorist English that would have Lord Macaulayâs approval. But jokes apart, all said and done, the recent protests were the first time I felt truly represented in Indian politics. This was a movement led by Gen Z folks who love playing FIFA, canât survive without air-conditioning, love burgers, delegate fasting to higher-ups, use parliamentary language that could have been lifted from an Anurag Kashyap film and celebrate their victories by dancing. This was much to the chagrin of their opponents and even some of their older allies, who couldnât understand why their thousand-word edits did not elicit the same response as Instagram reels. It had everything one would want in a popular movie: Bihari protesters demanding equal treatment with their Delhi brethren, including proper tear gas and water cannons ; a Salman Khan cameo ; a BDSM enthusiast from yesteryear keeping a maun vrat and then realising no one really cared; folks doing fit checks to see whether their outfits were suitable for Jantar Mantar aesthetics; unparliamentary words to describe leaders; and, finally, a concession from the powers that be, who donât concede. Beneath the carnival, however, lay a fairly straightforward grievance. Indians have a very high tolerance for inequities. We barely complain when potholes swallow us whole. We are fine traversing streets that make Takeshiâs Castle look like a stroll in the park. We breathe poisonous air that would give Darth Vader asthma. We file income tax returns for roads that destroy our carsâ suspension systems, assuming the cars survive ethanol blending. Perhaps this tolerance endured because we always had one escape route, one Stairway to Heaven, to borrow the words of Messrs Plant and Page: competitive examinations. The exam is the great Indian secular faith. Crack it, and all that glitters can be yours. It is one of the few institutions revered almost equally in every kind of household. Families reorganise their entire existence around one childâs preparation. Parents exhaust their savings on coaching institutes. Weddings, festivals and even family illnesses are expected to accommodate the examination calendar. The starting line was never equal. A richer child has private tutors, the privilege of knowing the grammar of the elite, a quiet room, good nutrition and several years of coaching. Yet the central promise endured: someone without those privileges could still make it through time, inclination, intelligence and extraordinary effort. IITian-turned-journalist Sandipan Deb captured the idea in his book The IITians , which described the graduates of independent Indiaâs first great educational institutions as âMidnightâs Brahminsâ. The phrase came from Congress leader and fellow IITian Jairam Ramesh, who saw the IITians as a new secular elite created after Indiaâs tryst with destiny, technocrats who replaced scripture with science. The sobriquet was meant for the IITs, but every competitive examination offered a version of the same promise. The right rank could vanquish generations of poverty. It could turn the child of a farmer, shopkeeper or government clerk into the CEO of a multinational company, a chief bureaucrat or a scientist landing a spacecraft on the âdark side of the Moonâ. It could transform the prospects of an entire family through the grit of one childâs intellect. Government exams are a purer version of this promise. The salary might be modest, but the job offers respect, security, status and pension, and the hope that the next generation will begin the race a few metres ahead. In vast parts of India, the appointment letter remained the most plausible instrument of social mobility ever invented. Then the dream began springing leaks. The NEET-UG controversy of 2024 , the cancellation of UGC-NET and numerous state-level recruitment scandals had already eroded trust. Each cancellation carries the cost of a train ticket, another year without earnings, another loan and the furrowed brows of parents waiting for the future to change. NEET-UG 2026 simply became the straw that broke the camelâs back, the leak epitomising the breakdown of a secret covenant between the student and the Republic. The powers that be responded with a method of communication that had become sui generis and had worked very well since 2014. Question the motivations of the protesters. Search for political forces behind them. Warn that anti-national elements might exploit the agitation. Use force. Turn the grievance into an ideological contest. Remind everyone of the Congressâs failures. Blame Nehru if required. The problem was that this time the old grammar did not fit the subject. Many of the protesters were genuinely non-political, simply angry at a future stolen. They had followed all the rules laid down by the state and were still being shortchanged. There is no ideological manifesto that can be removed, no demand for a revolution. The grievance was immediate, personal, painful and all too real for parents across the country. The other problem that the government faces is generational. Someone who is 21 today was nine when Narendra Modi became Prime Minister. Manmohan Singh, the Commonwealth Games scandal, 26/11, 2G, Anna Hazare and the arguments that propelled the BJP to power belong to a political prehistory they encountered through YouTube clips, WhatsApp forwards and relatives who still become animated whenever someone says âcoal allocationâ. This generation has never known the BJP as an insurgent force standing outside the establishment. For them, the BJP is the establishment. Congressâs failures are immaterial to them. Telling students âitâs better nowâ is akin to telling people in the 1960s that life was better post-British rule. Congressâs failures remain historically relevant. They have diminishing value as an answer to a leaked question paper in 2026. The new Gen Z has no memory of Congress rule; it did not live through it. It has grown up in a Digital India of instant payments, biometric identification, online applications and Mann Ki Baat. The system that gave us Digital India cannot suddenly plead administrative helplessness when a national examination collapses like a wave function. A political operation capable of monitoring every opposition remark, producing instant rebuttals and turning speeches into reels within minutes cannot explain that protecting a question paper is simply too complicated. The promise of supreme competence produced expectations of supreme competence. This does not make Gen Z one political species. This author happens to spend a lot of time with Gen Z, listening to their hopes, dreams and aspirations. Its members do not share one ideology, leader or cultural outlook. Many are culturally conservative, strongly nationalist and broadly sympathetic to the BJP. Others are liberal, Left-wing, apolitical or interested only in obtaining the job for which they have spent years preparing. Many prefer Dhurandhar and Rang De Basanti at the same time. Others recognise that they are both propaganda and yet enjoy them for their art. What unites them is a set of common conditions: expensive education, fierce competition, economic anxiety, uncertain employment and a lifetime spent under the same central government. When the familiar communication methods failed, senior Indian politicians attempted something even more ridiculous: speaking the language of Gen Z. The Prime Minister started making reels . Parliamentarians started saying âclocked itâ, âMIAâ, âFOMOâ and âdeluluâ . Perhaps the finest example of this changing conversation was a gym video in which youngsters discussed the protests through a thicket of catchphrases. One character blamed another for failing to âclockâ what India was like when they were ten before urging everyone to build their bodies and the country together. It was what the young folks call cringe. As former Rajya Sabha MP Priyanka Chaturvedi noted: âGen Z coded. Not.â BJP members and supporters, speaking privately, admitted that the approach was terribly ham-handed. The reel launched a thousand satirical responses, almost all of which were funnier than the original. The problem lay deeper than embarrassing slang. The government had mistaken a crisis of trust for a crisis of communication. Young people may still enjoy propaganda that confirms their beliefs, but they can recognise an uncle reciting internet slang from a briefing note, almost like the 30 Rock scene of Steve Buscemi with a backwards cap asking: âHow do you do, fellow kids?â Gen Zâs parents can be scared by the past, but the Gen Z revolution is not televised; itâs on Instagram Reels . It cannot be controlled with narratives. The algorithm is too mutinous and chaotic to control. The movementâs apparent frivolity made it harder for the political class to understand. The dancing, memes, fit checks, references and profanity led older observers to mistake a different aesthetic for a lack of seriousness. Itâs just a different medium of protest. Post-colonial scholars often argue that politeness is a symbol of colonial oppression. The lack of solemnity is a similar weapon. Mockery denies the government the battlefield it preferred. A television debate could portray an activist as dangerous, misinformed or politically compromised. A meme, on the other hand, can travel halfway around the globe before the news anchor has tied his shoelaces. Even if Dipke and Co became the face of the cockroach movement, the anger was collective. The opposition should be equally careful about reading the protests as an endorsement, irrespective of bypoll results. A generation with no meaningful memory of Congress in government has very little nostalgia for it. Anger against an incumbent does not automatically become affection for whoever occupies the opposition benches. Every party trying to communicate through borrowed slang risks receiving the same merciless treatment. For more than a decade, the governmentâs political genius lay in understanding the media environment better than its opponents. It mastered WhatsApp and social media even as its opponents depended on the established media to get their point across. But every successful playbook comes with an expiry date. Students donât need politicians to speak the lingo of Gen Z. They need an acceptance of their grievances, not ministers posting reels and saying âdeluluâ. History has shown that student protests, in particular, have a tendency to escape the boundaries initially drawn around them. In 19th-century China, Hong Xiuquan repeatedly failed the imperial civil service examinations, started imagining he was a brother of Jesus and eventually led the Taiping Rebellion, which established a rival state and took the Qing dynasty 15 years to crush at the cost of 20 million lives. Indiaâs experience is less apocalyptic, though no less instructive . Students participated in the movements that challenged British rule. After Independence, the anti-Hindi agitations transformed Tamil Naduâs political landscape. A protest over hostel food prices in Gujarat helped ignite the Nav Nirman movement. Student unrest in Bihar grew into Jayaprakash Narayanâs call for Sampoorna Kranti, challenged Indira Gandhi and produced a generation of leaders who continue to shape Indian politics. The Mandal protests of 1990 began on campuses, triggered tragic self-immolations and helped reorder the countryâs debate over caste, reservations and political representation. These movements shared little ideologically. What they shared was a pattern: a grievance the government considered containable became a vessel for much wider discontent. The Cockroach protests are neither the Taiping Rebellion nor the JP Movement. They might end as a remarkable five-week uprising followed by a ministerial resignation and a few administrative reforms. Yet governments have repeatedly discovered that student anger rarely remains confined to the classroom once it becomes a larger argument about fairness, opportunity and the legitimacy of the system itself. For years, Indiaâs students were told that their futures depended on clearing an examination. This summer, the Cockroaches forced the government to realise that it was being examined too. History is a strict invigilator. It seldom grants re-tests. And those who donât learn from history are condemned to repeat it. To borrow a line from the only songwriter to have won the Nobel Prize in Literature, âthe times they are a-changinââ. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: Women emerge as new shield for competitive exam fraud networks
text: Patna : A new and disturbing pattern has emerged in Bihar âs competitive examination fraud cases, with investigation agencies finding that exam mafias are increasingly using women as a shield to operate their solver networks. The Economic Offences Unit (EOU) has found the involvement of several women in alleged irregularities linked to the BPSC assistant public sanitation and waste management officer examination, assistant education development officer (AEDO), the havildar instructor recruitment examination and the NEET-UG re-examination controversy. Women were allegedly being used for multiple tasksâfrom entering examination centres and passing answer keys to candidates to collecting admit cards, storing digital evidence and even appearing as proxy candidates, according to the officials. One of the most significant revelations came during the BPSC assistant public sanitation and waste management officer examination at A N College in Patna on April 23, 2026. A woman biometric operator, Anshu Priya, was caught inside the examination hall while providing an answer key to candidate Roshan Kumar. A case was registered at S K Puri police station, following which the EOU took up the investigation. The EOU found that Anshu was in contact with alleged middleman Atul Raj Pandey, a biometric staff member, and an answer key had been sent to her through WhatsApp. Her questioning and the subsequent arrest of Atul helped investigators uncover the wider network. The person who allegedly sent the answer key to Anshu has also been identified and is being searched for. The arrest of alleged exam fixer Atul, who was working as a biometric operator at an examination centre in Kankarbagh, also brought another woman, Deepika Kumari, his colleague and a biometric staff member, under the scanner. She was also allegedly linked to the AEDO exam held between April 14 and 21, 2026. But it was cancelled after the examination paper allegedly leaked in Nalanda district. Forensic examination of a mobile phone seized from the examination centre revealed digital evidence linked to earlier examination fraud cases. The EOU is now investigating Deepikaâs alleged links with different members of the solver syndicate and determining how long she had been associated with the network. In the havildar instructor examination conducted by the Bihar Police Subordinate Services Commission (BPSSC) on July 29, investigators found the name of Riya Kumari during forensic analysis of the mobile phone of alleged middleman Raj Samdarshi alias Raja. According to the investigation, Riya had exchanged WhatsApp messages with Raja and allegedly sent him PDF files containing the admit cards of four candidates. She asked him which question set would be assigned to those candidates. Riya has been named as an accused in the case, and efforts are reportedly underway to arrest her. The investigation into the NEET-UG re-examination controversy has also brought two womenâMadhupuriya and Poonamâinto focus. The re-examination was conducted nationwide on June 21, 2026, following the cancellation of the original May 3 exam due to a major question paper leak and subsequent massive public and political uproar. Madhupuriya, who was a NEET aspirant, is reportedly the wife of alleged exam mafia operative Dr Ravishankar Samrat. Instead of appearing herself, a medical college student, Poonam, was caught taking the examination on her behalf. EOU found that Poonam had been promised Rs2 lakh, with Rs25,000 allegedly paid as an advance. Further investigation also indicated Madhupuriyaâs alleged involvement in another examination-related irregularity. ADG of EOU, Amit Kumar Jain, said, âThe examination racketeers might have started recruiting women because female personnel working inside examination centres may attract comparatively less suspicion from security personnel and static magistrates.â The syndicates allegedly exploit this perceived advantage by bringing women biometric operators, intermediaries and proxy candidates into their network. Jain added, âHowever, we donât differentiate between male and female accused. title: NEET protest FIRs quashed: CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke calls SC move âabsolute justiceâ
text: CJP's Abhijeet Dipke heralded this ruling as essential justice for all participants CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Tuesday welcomed the Supreme Courtâs decision to quash FIRs against students who took part in protests over the NEET paper leak, calling the order "absolute justice" and saying the ruling had delivered on the demands raised during the agitation. Speaking to reporters here, Dipke thanked the Supreme Court and said the decision had brought relief to students who protested at Jantar Mantar as well as families of those who died by suicide over the alleged paper leak. The Supreme Court on Tuesday quashed all FIRs registered against students who participated in the CJP-led protests between July 20 and 25 across the country, news agency PTI reported. A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant also directed the Centre to provide compensation within three months to the families of students who died by suicide over the NEET paper leak. "Our demands have been met. This is absolute justice. It took us a month (for this)," he said. CJP founder thanks SC, apologises to bereaved families Dipke said the outcome had been made possible by people's power and said he had been meeting several delegations over the issue. "I apologise to the families that we could not save your kids. We are very sorry that you lost your kids," the CJP convener said, referring to students who died by suicide. He blamed the government for the deaths and alleged that they were a result of the systemâs failure. The government, he said, had now accepted the demand for compensation to the families of students who died by suicide. "The government has accepted the demands but it has to take the responsibility that not a single student dies due to paper leak," he said. Dipke said the government must also ensure that no student loses their life because of shortcomings in the system. "We cannot afford this anymore," he said. NEET protests saw clashes in Delhi The CJP-led march in Delhi on July 20 witnessed clashes between protesters and security personnel, who used lathis and teargas shells to disperse demonstrators attempting to move towards Parliament. The student-led agitation, which spread to several cities, centred on demands including the resignation of then Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The protests had begun at Jantar Mantar on June 20. The agitation was called off on July 25 after Pradhan resigned and the government accepted the CJPâs other demands. title: HC allows 2 'linked' to NEET leak to go for counselling
text: The court was hearing the students' plea seeking release of their re-NEET results NEW DELHI: Delhi HC has directed National Testing Agency (NTA) to declare within 24 hours the NEET-UG re-examination results of two candidates, whose results were withheld over allegations linking them to the question paper leak. Justice Jasmeet Singh pointed out the candidates had not been named as accused by CBI in its chargesheet. While CBI told the court that it did not make them accused, though they had paid money to get question papers, the judge observed that at this stage, it was just an allegation and "therefore, the petitioners cannot be treated as persons against whom criminal culpability has been established or as having been found guilty of any illegality". Watch NTA Calls Viral NEET-UG OMR Sheets Fake, Warns Of Strict Legal Action The court was hearing the students' plea seeking release of their re-NEET results and permission to participate in the ongoing counselling. The CBI chargesheet named the two petitioners as witnesses, and not accused. NTA, however, issued show-cause notices to them and withheld their results. During the hearing, NTA submitted that it withheld the results after CBI informed it that several candidates had allegedly received or shared the question paper of the May 3 examination. On its part, CBI submitted that the petitioners had received the question paper and had the "mens rea" (intent) to commit the illegality, since money had been paid by them for obtaining the question paper. HC observed that the petitioners were at a "nascent stage of their academic careers", and withholding their results merely on the basis of allegations that were yet to be tested would cause serious prejudice to them. title: NEET PG 2026: PIB calls Jaipur paper leak reports misleading, re-exam set for 2,445 candidates
text: NEET PG 2026 re exam date The Press Information Bureau (PIB) has dismissed social media claims that the NEET PG 2026 question paper was leaked at an examination centre in Jaipur. In a fact-check issued after the examination, PIB said the viral claim was misleading and confirmed that there was no question paper leak during the NEET PG 2026 examination. The clarification comes after the test faced disruption at select centres in Jaipur, leaving thousands of candidates unable to complete their examination. The National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) has since announced a re-examination for the affected candidates. NEET PG 2026 paper leak claim is misleading, says PIB Social media posts had alleged that the NEET PG 2026 question paper was leaked from an examination centre in Jaipur. Addressing the claims, the PIB Fact Check unit said the information circulating online was misleading. According to the government fact-checking agency, there was no question paper leak during the NEET PG 2026 examination. Candidates have been advised not to rely on unverified social media posts and to check official communications before drawing conclusions about the examination. The PIB Fact Check unit has also encouraged the public to submit suspicious or misleading government-related claims for verification. Candidates can contact PIB Fact Check through WhatsApp at +91 8799711259 or email factcheck@pib.gov.in. What happened at the Jaipur NEET PG centre? The NEET PG 2026 examination was conducted on August 30 across the country. While the examination was completed successfully for the overwhelming majority of candidates, a technical disruption affected candidates appearing at the iON Digital Zone iDZ Sitapura Centres in Jaipur, Rajasthan. The disruption was caused by an internal power supply issue at the examination centres. As a result, 2,445 candidates could not complete the examination as scheduled. The incident appears to have triggered speculation online, with claims about a possible paper leak subsequently circulating on social media. PIB has now clarified that the disruption should not be confused with a question paper leak. NBEMS announces re-examination for affected candidates To ensure that candidates affected by the disruption are not disadvantaged, NBEMS has scheduled a fresh examination for all 2,445 candidates. The re-examination will be held on September 5, 2026, at 3 pm in Jaipur. The decision is intended to provide the affected candidates with an equal and fair opportunity to appear for the postgraduate medical entrance examination. The re-test is particularly significant because the interruption was not caused by any action on the part of the candidates. Conducting a separate examination allows the authorities to address the disruption without compromising the fairness of the admission process. Candidates who are eligible for the re-examination should follow the instructions issued by NBEMS and monitor the official communication for details regarding the examination centre, reporting time and other requirements. NEET PG 2026 examination held across 339 cities The NEET PG 2026 examination was scheduled for 2,73,096 candidates at 1,111 examination centres across 339 cities covering all 36 States and Union Territories. According to the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, 2,65,980 candidates appeared for the examination. The test was successfully completed for approximately 2,63,535 candidates. The Jaipur disruption therefore affected a relatively small section of the overall candidate pool, although the impact on those candidates was significant enough to warrant a separate examination. When will NEET PG 2026 result be announced? The NEET PG 2026 result is expected to be announced by September 15, 2026. However, NBEMS has not officially confirmed the result date so far. Candidates should therefore treat September 15 only as an expected timeline and wait for an official announcement before considering the date final. The result will be important for candidates seeking admission to postgraduate medical programmes, including MD and MS courses, as their ranks will determine their options during the subsequent counselling process. NEET PG 2026 paper analysis: Moderate difficulty, clinical focus Initial reactions to the NEET PG 2026 question paper suggest that the examination was of moderate difficulty. Students and experts reported that the paper placed considerable emphasis on clinical application rather than straightforward factual recall. Several questions reportedly focused on areas such as image-based diagnosis, investigations, treatment strategies and clinical decision-making. The nature of the paper meant that candidates needed to apply their understanding of medical concepts to clinical situations. This made conceptual clarity and practical understanding important alongside knowledge of factual information. title: Gen Z protests in India: Who do we really blame?
text: File photo: Gen Z protesters Delhiâs Jantar Mantar has seen its biggest youth demonstrations in years. What started in early June as anger over the NEET paper leak and CBSE marking irregularities snowballed into a nationwide Gen Z movement â one big enough to force the resignation of the Union Education Minister. Tear gas, baton charges, an indefinite hunger strike, hundreds injured â and at the center of it all, thousands of students who simply said: this system cheated us . Itâs tempting to treat this as a story about one leaked paper or one minister. It isnât. The paper leak was the spark. The real fire has been building for decades, inside classrooms, teacher training colleges, and education ministries that never quite got their priorities straight. If weâre serious about asking âwho to blame,â we have to look upstream â much further upstream than a single exam scandal. 1. A No-Fail Policy That Let a Generation Coast For nearly five decades, Indian school education has quietly operated on one unspoken theme: nobody should fail in school. Continuous promotion policies, diluted assessments, and a deep institutional discomfort with telling a child âyou need to try harderâ have produced students who reach Class 10 or 12 without ever being tested against a real standard. The tragic irony is that this âkindnessâ simply outsources the failure to a later, harsher stage of life â the entrance exam, the job interview, the first year of college, the workplace. We didnât eliminate failure. We postponed it, compounded it, and handed it to 18-year-olds all at once, in the highest-stakes moments of their lives. Is it any surprise that a generation raised on artificial success is now enraged when the real world â and a rigged, leak-prone exam system â finally hands them an honest, brutal verdict? 2. A Curriculum Frozen in an Earlier Century Walk into most classrooms and youâll find a curriculum that has barely kept pace with a world being reshaped by AI, automation, and constantly shifting industry demands. Pedagogy remains largely lecture-and-memorize, disconnected from problem-solving, critical thinking, or any real linkage to what employers actually need. Students spend twelve-plus years memorizing content for exams that have little bearing on employability, then discover â often only after graduation â that the market wants skills nobody taught them. That gap between classroom and career is precisely the kind of betrayal that turns quiet frustration into street protest. 3. Teacher Training That Trains Nobody for Todayâs Classroom You cannot fix school education without fixing the pipeline that produces teachers. Indiaâs B.Ed programs remain largely unreformed â outdated in content, mechanical in method, and almost entirely disconnected from modern classroom needs or child psychology. Worse, thereâs no serious, independent mechanism to evaluate the quality of school education itself. Boards conduct exams; they rarely audit outcomes. Without robust, transparent quality checks, a school can look functional on paper while failing its students in practice â and no one is meaningfully accountable for it. Paper leaks and marking irregularities arenât isolated glitches; theyâre what happens when a system has never built strong evaluation and integrity mechanisms in the first place. 4. Ministers Who Regulate Private Schools Instead of Fixing Government Ones Perhaps the most telling failure is one of political will. Education ministers across states have often found it easier to tighten regulations on private schools â fee caps, admission rules, compliance paperwork â than to do the harder, slower work of improving government schools, where the majority of Indiaâs children actually study. Regulation without reform is political theater. It signals âactionâ without addressing the actual quality deficit â the teacher shortages, crumbling infrastructure, poor learning outcomes, and now, exam systems fragile enough to leak. When students finally rebelled this year, they werenât just protesting a leaked paper. They were protesting fifty years of a system that optimized for appearances over outcomes. 5. The Employability Verdict: 80% Unemployable, and Rising Anger to Match Perhaps the most damning evidence of all is what happens after students leave this system. Over the years, multiple industry studies â from NASSCOMâs employability surveys to various National Employability Reports â have consistently pegged the number of Indian graduates considered unemployable by industry standards anywhere between 75% and 85%, depending on the sector and the year of the study. Whichever exact figure you pick, the message is the same: four in five of our âeducatedâ youth are not equipped to actually work in the industries they trained for. Think about what that really means. We spend a decade and a half putting a child through a no-fail school system, an outdated curriculum, and a college pipeline staffed by teachers trained on equally outdated B.Ed programs â and at the end of it, industry looks at 80% of the output and says, ânot usable.â That isnât a minor mismatch. Thatâs a systemic failure to prepare an entire generation for the one thing school is supposed to prepare them for: a livelihood. And so, in a strange and tragic way, we have prepared our youth well â just not for the purpose we intended. We built a system efficient at producing degrees, disillusionment, and frustration, but not employability. We equipped them with just enough grievance, energy, and idle time to fill Jantar Mantar, but not enough real skill or opportunity to channel that same energy into building the âViksit Bharatâ â a developed India â that every political leader loves to invoke in speeches. The protest on the street is not a distraction from that dream. It is the direct, predictable output of a system that never seriously built toward it. 6. Two Kinds of Youth, Two Very Different Futures And yet, watching the protest videos themselves raises another, uncomfortable question. Scroll through the footage and the sheer amount of crude, abusive language on display is hard to miss. Itâs a jarring reminder that a movement built on legitimate grievances can just as easily curdle into something else â not a disciplined push toward reform, but a slide toward mob anger and anarchy, if it isnât channeled with purpose and restraint. Contrast that with another set of young Indians making headlines for very different reasons. Companies like Skyroot Aerospace â founded by twenty-somethings who cut their teeth fighting Indiaâs notorious red tape, licensing delays, and regulatory inertia â are building world-class rockets and joining the countryâs unicorn club anyway. That is what the same raw youthful energy looks like when itâs pointed at building rather than burning down. The contrast is the whole point. Both sets of young Indians came out of the same broken education system. One channel of that energy is heading toward disruption without direction; the other is heading toward Viksit Bharat. The difference isnât talent â India clearly has no shortage of that. The difference is values, aptitude, attitude, and adaptability â precisely the things our schools have never been designed to build. If we want more Skyroots and fewer street clashes, the fix has to start at the root: an education system that deliberately instills character and capability, not just degrees. The Bigger Picture None of this excuses corruption, negligence, or exam malpractice â those deserve accountability on their own terms. But the anger seen on Delhiâs streets, the hunger strike, the memes mocking a government once thought untouchable â all of it reflects something deeper than outrage over one leak. Itâs the accumulated frustration of a generation that was told it would never fail in school, only to find out the hard way that the world outside doesnât grade on the same curve. If governments want this to be the last such protest rather than the first of many, the fix canât stop at a resignation or a new exam protocol. It has to start with honest assessment in schools, curriculum overhaul, serious teacher training reform, and real accountability for public education â not just tighter rules for private players. A note on framing: this piece argues one reading of the crisis â that systemic education failures , not just administrative corruption, are the root cause. Others closer to the movement point to different or additional culprits: entrenched political corruption, weak institutional oversight of exam bodies, a broader jobs crisis affecting even skilled graduates, and a wider âGen Z vs. establishmentâ wave visible across many countries right now. Any full accounting of âwho to blameâ probably includes all of the above. Disclaimer : Views expressed above are the author's own.

title: SC quashes FIRs against all NEET protesters, but 'hardened criminals' to face trial; CJP reacts
text: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Tuesday invoked its special powers and quashed all FIRs registered against student protesters in different parts of the country during the NEET paper leak protests. The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana said the order had been passed in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case and shall not be treated as a precedent. The apex court said it was invoking its special powers under Article 142 of the Constitution considering the future of the students who bona fide participated in the protests. Watch â48 Hours Or Sit-Inâ: Abhijeet Dipke Warns After CJP Team Allegedly Attacked Near Jaipur School The court, however, allowed Delhi Police to pursue the FIR against 2,873 individuals who were present at the Jantar Mantar protests, citing their serious criminal antecedents. This comes a day after the Centre moved the apex court seeking to quash FIRs registered against student protesters over alleged violence during protests against the NEET paper leak in Delhi and other states. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, appearing for the Centre and Delhi Police, also informed the apex court that the Centre remained committed to fulfilling all three assurances given to CJP leaders during their meeting with the government. Under the first assurance, the Centre would not pursue FIRs registered between July 20 and July 25. The second was that no fresh FIRs would be registered in connection with the matter. The third assurance was that the government would provide compensation to the families of students who died by suicide allegedly in connection with the NEET paper leak. "The Centre is committed to honouring the assurance given to CJP leaders to provide compensation to the families of students who died by suicide after the NEET exam cancellation; however, three months are needed to work out the modalities," Mehta told the Supreme Court. "As of now, we are committed to fulfilling all three assurances," he added. Following the apex court hearing, Cockroach Janata Party called off its September 5 protest against the Centre for failing to honour the promises made to persuade the group to withdraw the agitation. "I want to state that in view of the positive assurances of the Government of India and the judicial sanctity bestowed upon them today, and in view of the order being passed by this court, the CJP deems it appropriate to withdraw the call for the march on September 5 and looks forward to compliance with today's order," CJP co-convener Sourav Das said during a hearing in the Supreme Court. How CJP reacted After the hearing, Das said welcomed SC's order but also questioned why were these 'hardend criminals' allowed to roam freely in the society in the first place. "Regarding the Delhi Policeâs apprehension, based on facial recognition technology, that around 2,800 alleged hardened criminals were present at the protest site, we argued during negotiations with the government that if these 2,800 hardened criminals were indeed present, the first question was why they were roaming freely in society in the first place," Das said while talking to reporters. title: âMurder by systemâ: CJPâs Abhijeet Dipke blames govt for MPSC aspirant's death; flags paper leaks, unemployment
text: Abhijeet Dipke has called the suicide of an MPSC aspirant a murder by the very system they sought to navigate PUNE: Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Thursday blamed the government and what he described as a failing competitive-exam system for the death of MPSC aspirant Prathamesh Deshmukh, calling the suicide a "murder done by the system" and demanding steps to ensure such incidents do not recur. Dipke, who visited Deshmukh's family in Khasapuri village in Dharashiv, also linked the debate over reservation to the lack of quality education and employment opportunities, alleging that young people were losing faith in the government. Dipke links death to MPSC system, unemployment Deshmukh, 28, who was preparing for Maharashtra Public Service Commission (MPSC) examinations, allegedly died by suicide in Pune. A note recovered from him mentioned a debt of around Rs 2.5 lakh. A native of Paranda in Dharashiv, Deshmukh had been staying in a rented accommodation in Navi Peth while preparing for competitive examinations, news agency PTI reported. Speaking to reporters after meeting his family, Dipke said Deshmukh had gone to Pune hoping to secure a government job and improve his family's financial condition. "He borrowed money from friends to meet his expenses. But due to paper leaks and delayed results, pressure mounted on students. This (Deshmukh's suicide) is system's fault and it is a murder done by the system," he alleged. Dipke said Deshmukh's death reflected the pressure faced by unemployed youth, particularly those from rural areas, because of financial hardship and what he called failures in the examination system. "Prathamesh stayed in Pune and used to have a meal only once a day due to his financial condition. According to his mother, Prathamesh used to say that he would come home in a government car, but unfortunately he was brought here in an ambulance yesterday. His father has already passed away," Dipke said. âHow will rural youth survive in Pune?â Dipke said aspirants coming to Pune from villages often struggle to pay for accommodation, food, coaching and library facilities while preparing for competitive examinations. "He (Deshmukh) had borrowed Rs 2 lakh to Rs 2.5 lakh from his friends...A youth had to end his life for this much amount. This is the condition of our youth in rural areas because there is no employment," he said. "Prathamesh was preparing for MPSC exams and we all know what is happening in the MPSC. Exams are not conducted properly, the results are improper and paper leaks also take place. How will the youth from rural areas survive in a city like Pune? How will they pay the money required for library, food, rent and coaching? This is a question that haunts the youth from rural areas," he said. He also spoke about the difficulty students face in returning home after spending years preparing for government examinations, PTI reported. ''Prathamesh left the village with a dream to become an officer, then how can he return without cracking the exams? For this, he did everything that he could. He stayed there (in Pune) for four years by curtailing his expenses. There are thousands of youths like him,'' he said. Dipke links reservation demand to lack of opportunities Turning to the reservation issue, Dipke argued that stronger public education and employment opportunities would reduce the demand for quotas. "The government cannot give good facilities. If they get good facilities, good schools and education and opportunities, why would anyone ask for reservation? People are asking for reservation because the government has completely failed in giving quality education and providing jobs. People have lost faith in the government so they are seeking constitutional remedies," he said. CJP to join MPSC aspirantsâ agitation Dipke said the CJP had earlier extended support to MPSC aspirants but would now participate directly in their agitation. "The government should be alert and incidents like (suicide by) Prathamesh should not recur as it cannot be tolerated any more. Till now, we extended our support to the MPSC aspirants who were agitating. But what I have seen here today, we cannot let such cases happen any further. Therefore we have decided to get into this agitation," he said. Dipke's remarks came after his visit to Khasapuri, where he met Deshmukh's grieving family members. text: Gaurav Bhatia has sought a permanent injunction against the CJP and its leaders, besides claiming Rs 2 crore in damages. NEW DELHI: BJP national spokesperson and senior advocate Gaurav Bhatia has approached the Delhi high court seeking Rs 2 crore in damages from Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka over alleged defamatory social media posts. The defamation suit, which also names the CJP as a defendant, is scheduled to come up before the HC on Wednesday. Watch BJP's Gaurav Bhatia Files â¹2 Crore Defamation Case Against CJP Leaders Over Controversial X Post Bhatia also announced the legal action on his X handle, posting: âTomorrow, every solid argument will echo in the court. The final nail will be hammered into the coffin of lies." Das responded to Bhatia's post with a taunt in Hindi: âHilte dulte Greater Noida court matt poch jana!â The legal dispute centres on social media posts by the CJP and its leaders that allegedly circulated a graphic containing a statement falsely attributed to Bhatia. The lawsuit further alleged that the CJP and its leaders have repeatedly made comments that lower the dignity and authority of the judiciary. Bhatia has sought a permanent injunction against the CJP and its leaders, besides claiming Rs 2 crore in damages. title: Notice served to Noida law student for attending CJP protest, then revoked
text: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters during a demonstration at Jantar Mantar on July 20 Noida: A second-year Gautam Buddha University (GBU) student was served a notice on Sept 4 for allegedly spreading anti-govt information and instigating students to participate in a protest organised by Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhiâs Jantar Mantar over NEET exam paper leaks in July. The notice was cancelled on Sept 5 after a police inquiry found the information on which it was based to be false. The notice, issued by an executive magistrate under BNSS Section 130 on Sept 4, stated that a report submitted by Ecotech 1 station house officer Arvind Verma and a sub-inspector alleged that Akshat Tripathi, a second-year LLB student of the university, was involved in spreading anti-govt information and encouraging students to join the CJP protest that created âconsiderable tensionâ on campus and a possibility of a confrontation, which could disturb public peace and order. It asked Tripathi to explain why he should not be directed to furnish a personal bond of Rs 5 lakh and two sureties of an equal amount, undertaking that he would maintain peace for six months. The orders were issued under BNSS sections 126 (to show cause why they should not execute a bond or bail bond for keeping the peace) and 135 (inquiry into the truth of information for keeping public peace). Section 130 allows a magistrate to issue a formal written order when asking a person to show cause to maintain peace or good behaviour. On Tuesday, police clarified the proceedings did not continue after they visited his Noida house and conducted an enquiry into the allegations. An official told TOI the information in the initial report was found to be false, following which the notice was cancelled on Sept 5, and no action was taken against the student. Tripathi, meanwhile, told TOI that he left the GBU campus on May 25 for a three-month semester break. âDuring this entire period, I was in Allahabad. On July 20, I attended the CJP protest in Delhiâs Jantar Mantar. I fail to understand the basis on which such a notice has been issued to me,â he said. âIf I was not present on campus during the period in question, and the university itself was closed for the semester break, on what basis have these allegations been made against me?â Tripathi claimed he had not received any notice revoking the Sept 4 order yet. The notice also drew criticism from Students Federation of India (SFI), which described it as a ârepressive actionâ by govt and UP Police. âQuestioning govt and demanding accountability is now a crime in India,â Partha Sarathi Dwivedi, SFI state president, said. title: BJP stays on top, Congress gets a warning: What Rajasthan civic polls mean for 2028 assembly elections
text: Civic poll results were announced for Rajasthan wards today. NEW DELHI: The Rajasthan civic poll results have reinforced the dominance of the ruling BJP despite some setbacks, brought cheers to the AAP and the CPM, but has rung alarm bells for the Congress ahead of the 2028 assembly elections in the state. The BJP has lost some ground, but the Congress has not gained all of it. Parties like AAP and the CPM have sprung surprise in some districts at the expense of the Congress. The AAP has emerged the winner in Baran Nagar Parishad, while the CPM has gained majority in Nokha Nagar Palika. The ruling BJP led the Congress in the Rajasthan urban local body elections, winning over 4,179 wards against the opposition party's 3,613 as results for at least 10,200 wards were declared. Independents put up a strong performance across the state, winning 2,273 wards, emerging as a potentially decisive force in several urban bodies. In a post on X, PM Modi said the results reflected support for the BJPâs policies of development and good governance under the âdouble-engine governmentâ. âHeartfelt thanks to the people of Rajasthan for delivering a resounding victory to the BJP in the municipal elections. This is a testament to the triumph of truth over the jhooth ki goonj (echo of lies),â PM Modi wrote. Shot in the arm for Bhajan Lal Sharma government The results are a shot in the arm for chief minister Bhajan Lal Sharma. Sharma was picked up by the BJP to lead the Rajasthan government, ignoring the claims of heavyweights like Vasundhara Raje, after the party won the 2023 assembly elections against the Congress. The BJP would be happy that despite the loss of some ground, overall it has dominated across the state. The chief minister would especially be satisfied with the results as it comes in the backdrop of several controversies that had cropped up in the recent past. The NEET paper leak expose, the Karni Sena protest over UGC regulations and the CJP campaign against the state of government schools were some of the issues that had put the state government on the backfoot. But the results show that these issues may have had a limited impact on the partyâs electoral prospects. Chief minister Bhajanlal Sharma thanked the voters for placing their trust in the party. "Today, I express my sincere gratitude to the people of Rajasthan for the historic and magnificent victory achieved by the Bharatiya Janata Party in the stateâs municipal body elections. I also thank all the party workers who dedicated their time and effort to secure this victory. I dedicate this triumph to them and to the people of Rajasthan, and offer them my congratulations and best wishes. The people of Rajasthan have endorsed the historic work accomplished in the state over the past two and a half years under the leadership of our Prime Minister Narendra Modi. They have embraced the Prime Ministerâs vision of a âViksit Bharatâ and a âViksit Rajasthan,â he said. The CM also thanked the youth of Rajasthan for placing their trust in Prime Minister Narendra Modi and claimed that his government had, in the past two and a half years, fulfilled 78% of the pledges it made to the public. Mixed bag for Congress The Congress has also made significant gains in some key civic bodies, but the party should be worried about AAP and CPM entering the opposition space and making gains at its expense. The victory of AAP in Baran and CPM in Nokha should be warning bells for the Congress which has been the dominant challenger and only alternative to the ruling BJP. Reacting to the verdict, state Congress president Govind Singh Dotasra said, "When local elections happen, most votes tend to go in favour of the ruling power. This has been the trend for a long time. But this time, the BJP has been completely wiped out. In the Lok Sabha, more than 50% of their votes were there, and today they've dropped to within 34-35%.â Dostara accused the BJP of engaging in dishonest practices in the wards and delimitation. âIn a major city like Jaipur, within the municipal corporation, Congress is ahead of the Bharatiya Janata Party in total votes by a margin of 10,000 votes. So, if we assess just the Jaipur Municipal Corporation, the BJP is behind Congress by 60-65 thousand votes. The vote percentage between Congress and the Bharatiya Janata Partyâwhenever the BJP was in power, it used to be around 9% ahead. Last time when we were in government, we were ahead by 2-2.5%. The misgovernance they've delivered, the public has shown them the mirror... In the 10 municipal corporations where the Chief Minister went, they managed a majority in only four, and that too due to dishonest delimitation; in the remaining 6, the majority is with Independents and Congress, not the Bharatiya Janata Party. This shows that this government has completely failed. Panchayat Raj elections are coming up, and in those, the Bharatiya Janata Party will face twice the debacle," the state Congress chief claimed. Dotasra also alleged that the Congress would have won around 1,500 more wards but for irregular and "unfair" delimitation of wards. He said the Congress won 542 wards reserved for Scheduled Castes, against 350 won by the BJP. In SC women-reserved wards, he said the Congress won 261 seats compared with 186 by the BJP, while in ST women-reserved wards, the Congress won 53 against the BJP's 39. Dotasra said the Congress won 37 of 80 wards in Ajmer, against 32 won by the BJP. Decisive Congress victory in Vasundhara Rajeâs bastion The Congress registered a decisive victory in the Jhalawar Municipal Council, winning 18 of its 25 wards in a region considered a political stronghold of former Rajasthan chief minister and senior BJP leader Vasundhara Raje. BJP national vice president Vasundhara Raje is the sitting BJP MLA from Jhalrapatan assembly constituency of Jhalawar district. The district has a total of eight urban local bodies. The Congress also delivered a major blow to the BJP in the Pali Municipal Corporation, turning the party's traditional stronghold into a closely contested political battleground. Pali is the home district of Rajasthan BJP President Madan Rathore, who has served as the party's Pali district president several times and was a two-time MLA from Sumerpur. In a significant setback for the BJP, the Congress not only emerged as the single largest party in the 65-member Municipal Corporation but also defeated the BJP in Rathore's own ward. Boost for AAP The AAP would be very happy with its victory in Baran. The party won 31 of the 60 wards, crossing the majority mark on its own. The Congress was a distant second with 18 wards and the BJP nine, while Independents secured two seats. The result will be a big boost for Arvind Kejriwalâs party given the fact that it has limited presence in the state. The BJP had won 115 seats with a vote share of 41.7%. The Congress claims that BJPâs Lok Sabha vote share fell 15 percentage points. This will be clear only after the final results and vote divisions are out. While the BJP will look to plug its weaknesses, the Congress will also go back to the drawing board and rework its strategy for the next state elections. In the 2023 assembly elections, the Congress had won 70 seats with a vote share of 39.58%. However, for now it has a bigger challenge at hand- to beat the BJP in wooing Independents where the party has emerged as the single largest party but could not gain majority. title: NTA issues important advisory on grievances; check what candidates need to include
text: NTA issues important advisory on grievances The National Testing Agency ( NTA ) has issued an advisory asking candidates to provide complete details when submitting grievances. The agency said that including the required information will help officials identify the candidate and address the issue more quickly. In an advisory shared on social media, NTA said it receives a large number of grievances every day through email and social media platforms. However, many complaints do not contain basic information needed to identify the candidate. With lakhs of candidates appearing for different examinations, the agency said it can be difficult to trace an individual application when important details are missing. NTA grievance advisory : What details should candidates provide? NTA has asked candidates to follow these instructions while submitting a complaint: Send the grievance from the registered email ID used while filling out the application form. Mention the Application Number in the subject line of the email. Clearly mention the name of the examination related to the complaint. Briefly explain the issue or concern. Attach relevant screenshots or supporting documents, if required. Send the complaint only to the dedicated helpdesk email address of the concerned examination. The helpdesk email address is available in the respective examination's information bulletin and on the official NTA website. Why has NTA issued the advisory? NTA handles a large number of applications for national-level entrance and recruitment examinations. The agency said that complaints without identifying information make it harder for officials to locate the relevant application and provide a timely response. Candidates are therefore advised to provide all the required details when raising a grievance. This can help officials identify the application without having to seek additional information from the candidate. Earlier, before the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test Undergraduate (NEET UG) re-test held on June 21, NTA had launched a live public grievance portal to address rumours related to paper leaks. The portal allowed aspirants and other stakeholders to report suspicious activities, including fake websites, fraudulent claims about question paper leaks and people falsely claiming to be NTA officials. title: 'Kept on ventilator': Congress flags delay in proroguing Parliament, links it to delimitation Bills
text: File photo: Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh NEW DELHI: Congress on Monday questioned the delay in proroguing Parliamentâs Monsoon Session, with party general secretary Jairam Ramesh alleging that the government was keeping the session open while seeking the numbers needed to pass the Delimitation Bills. Parliamentâs Monsoon Session began on July 20 and was adjourned sine die on August 13 after 19 sittings. Ramesh said 25 days had passed since the adjournment, but Parliament had still not been prorogued. Watch CM Vijay Urges PM Modi To Keep Lok Sabha Strength At 543, Opposes Population-Based Delimitation âToday is exactly 25 days since Parliament was adjourned sine die. But it has still NOT been prorogued,â Ramesh said in a post on X. He said prorogation normally takes place three to four days after a session is adjourned sine die, while citing the 28-day gap during the 2015 Monsoon Session as an earlier example. Ramesh links delay to delimitation Bills Ramesh referred to the 2015 session, which he said had been largely disrupted over the Lalit Modi issue. He alleged that the then Modi government had kept that session alive in the hope of passing the GST Bills, which required a two-thirds majority in the Rajya Sabha. He said the government was subsequently forced to consult the opposition more meaningfully before the Bills were passed later. Ramesh alleged that this yearâs Monsoon Session was being kept open because the Union home minister was seeking a two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha for the Delimitation Bills. âThe 2026 Monsoon Session has been kept on ventilator because the home minister is still scrambling around for his super-tainted two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha to get the Delimitation Bills passed,â he said. âHow much longer before he accepts the reality that his politics of threats and intimidation has reached its limit?â Ramesh added. The remarks came after the government faced a setback in the Lok Sabha in April over a Constitution Amendment Bill related to delimitation and implementation of women's reservation. What happened during the Monsoon Session During the Monsoon Session, 12 bills were passed by Parliament, while 11 bills were introduced in the Lok Sabha and two in the Rajya Sabha. Only the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026, was debated in the House, while the remaining Bills were passed without discussion amid opposition protests over issues including the NEET paper leak, alleged theft of Ram Temple donations and the police action against student protesters on July 20. title: 'Bones will mend but shattered dreams?' Rahul Gandhi meets Bihar students shot at during protest
text: Rahul Gandhi with injured student protesters NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Sunday shared a video of his interaction with three students who were injured during police action amid recent student protests in Bihar. The three were part of a group of students from Bihar who met the Lok Sabha leader of opposition at his Delhi residence on September 3. In a social media post, Gandhi said the three students had been âshot atâ, referring to a protest in Siwan, Bihar, on July 25. Watch Rahul Gandhi Slams BJP-RSS Over Kharge âShuddhikaranâ, Demands Action Under SC/ST Act âThink about it: what crime had these children committed that they were shot? They had asked the government for just three things â education, employment, and accountability,â the Raebareli MP wrote on X. The leg bone of one of the students, he added, was shattered after he was hit by a bullet fired from an AK-47. âAlong with it, his dream of joining the Army and serving the country was shattered too. Bullets tore through the shoulders of two other students,â Rahul Gandhi wrote. âThey were not criminals. They were children from poor families who had gone out to study carrying the dreams of their families â some wanted a good job, while others wanted to change the circumstances of their homes,â he added. The Congress leader further remarked that while their physical wounds would heal, there is no answer to how the psychological trauma they had suffered could be treated. "Mr prime minister, Mr chief minister â their broken bones will heal. Can you give them back their broken dreams?" Rahul Gandhi said, questioning Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Bihar chief minister Samrat Choudhary. Several parts of Bihar witnessed student protests, some of which turned violent, on July 25 as part of a broader agitation by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) in Delhi. The CJP was leading protests demanding the resignation of then-Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET paper leak issue, along with reforms in the education system. title: Centre moves Supreme Court to quash FIRs against NEET protesters
text: Centre seeks SC intervention over FIRs against NEET protesters NEW DELHI: The Centre has moved Supreme Court seeking to quash the FIRs registered against protesters in connection with alleged violence during protests over the NEET paper leak in Delhi and other states. Solicitor general Tushar Mehta mentioned the plea before a bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Monday, seeking the courtâs intervention in the matter, news agency ANI reported. The Centre has urged the Supreme Court to exercise its extraordinary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution to quash the FIRs registered against the protesting students. title: HC relief for Pune aspirant after RE-NEET-UG-2026 result withheld at CBIâs behest
text: High court Pune: National Testing Agency (NTA) on Thursday declared the RE-NEET-UG-2026 result of a Pune student (18) to enable him participate in the revised Centralised Admission Process (CAP) Round-I for the MBBS/BDS courses in the state quota, acting on an interim order of Bombay high court. The testing agency had withheld the studentâs result after CBI , probing the NEET-UG-2026 paper leak case, objected to declaration of his result based on the allegation that he was among the âdirect beneficiariesâ of the leaked paper. Advocate Pooja Thorat, representing the petitioner, told TOI , âThe student has been declared as qualified for the admission rounds. He will be a part of the CAP over the next two days.â The admission process ends on Aug 29. The HC bench of Justice R I Chagla and Justice Firdosh P Pooniwalla said on Aug 25, ââ¦ We are not coming in the way of the CBI proceedings, which shall be pursued by the CBI. Further, we are not making any observation as to the role played by the petitioner in the NEET 2026 examination as that is not within the purview of this court in presently considering the writ petition, considering the interim relief sought for by the petitioner. â On May 12, NTA cancelled the NEET-UG 2026 exam held on May 3 in the wake of a paper leak. It conducted the RE-NEET-UG-2026 on June 21 and declared the results on July 16. In its chargesheet filed on July 20, CBI did not name the Pune student as an accused and referred him among witnesses, along with similarly placed other students. Thorat told TOI , âWe brought to the courtâs notice two orders passed on Aug 21 by the principal bench (Mumbai) and the Nagpur bench that considered similar requests for declaration of results to enable the petitioners concerned participate in the CAP. The only difference between those and our matter was that the CBI objected to the declaration of result in our case.â The CBI maintained its objection and sought time to file an affidavit in reply to the petition. The NTA said it acted at the behest of CBI objecting to the declaration of result. The bench said the prior orders passed by the principal bench and the Nagpur bench were required to be considered as they had taken a view that, in the event, the petitioners had not been named as accused and only appear as witnesses in the chargesheet, indulgence was required to be shown to the petitioners. âThe objection is that the petitioner is a direct beneficiary of the leaked papers in the aforesaid NEET 2026 examination. This would be required to be established in the proceedings instituted by CBI,â the bench said. title: Javed Akhtar says he's proud of Shabana Azmi for joining protests at Jantar Mantar against NEET paper leak: 'This isn't the first time, when our relationship was developing, this is what she was involved in'
text: Javed Akhtar recently opened up about his wife Shabana Azmiâs long-standing commitment to speaking out against injustice, saying he feels âproudâ of her for joining the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in New Delhi last month. While several Bollywood personalities voiced their support for the protesting students online, Azmi chose to be present at Jantar Mantar, standing alongside students demanding action over the alleged leak of National Eligibility Entrance Test (NEET) papers. âThis isnât the first time sheâs done this. Sheâs aged now, so does it less now,â Akhtar said with a laugh during a recent interview on the podcast Lets Talk With DevnaG. Watch Javed Akhtar Questions MEA's Passport Remark; Government Issues Clarification Azmiâs participation came despite the risks involved. Following the Delhi Policeâs use of tear gas against protesters on July 20, the veteran actor suffered an asthma attack. She was subsequently diagnosed with the H1N1 virus, which kept her from taking part in student protests in Mumbai a few days later. Recalling her history of activism, Akhtar said, âIâve gone to the police station to bail her out. Sheâs gone for a hunger strike in Mumbai. Sheâs been quite active,â he said. âWhen our relationship was developing, this is what she was involved in.â The couple began dating in the late 1970s, after Akhtar met Azmi at the Mumbai residence of his family friend and celebrated poet Kaifi Azmi, who was Shabanaâs father. Akhtar also remembered the conversation he had with Azmi before she travelled to Delhi for the protests. âShe called me when I was in London to tell me sheâs going to Delhi for the protests. When she told me, I knew she would. Itâs the call of the conscience. Not once I told her to not go or think twice. The moment she told me I cannot not go, I knew the old Shabana had woken up, and nobody can stop her. And good she did! Iâm proud of her,â he said. Azmiâs activism stretches back decades. One of the most notable instances came in 1993, when she joined slum residents in Mumbaiâs Cuffe Parade to protest the demolition of their homes. She was arrested along with 16 others and reportedly refused both bail and acceptance of the charges against her. Her arrest even created an unusual situation involving her stage commitments. Her mother, veteran actor Shaukat Kaifi, had to persuade the police to escort Azmi to Tata Theatre so she could perform in the acclaimed play Tumhari Amrita while still in detention. Azmi arrived on stage wearing the dusty clothes in which she had been arrested. Eventually, Akhtar stepped in and bailed her out. Reflecting on why they continue to speak up despite the fear that can accompany activism, Akhtar said, âItâs not like we donât feel scared. We feel scared most of the times. But in some moments, youâve to get over the fear and have to call a spade a spade. Otherwise you wonât be able to look into the mirror. If I donât, I have no loyalty with either my zameen, zamana or zameer (land, time, and conscience). I donât do it much, but when your conscience is pushed against the wall, you have to do it,â he added. Azmi herself had previously revealed that her decision to attend the CJP protests came after she and Akhtar first attempted to address the matter through official channels. The couple wrote to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, asking him to meet with the students protesting over the NEET controversy. Although they received an acknowledgement that their letter had been received, they heard nothing further for three days. With no response forthcoming, Azmi decided to take matters into her own hands and join the protesters in person â continuing a decades-long pattern of activism that Akhtar says remains an integral part of who she is. title: 10 IPS, 3 IAS officers shifted; former Siwan SP gets posting
text: Patna : Bihar govt on Friday transferred 10 IPS, three IAS and as many BPS officers. Besides, three IAS officers were given additional charges and two were relieved from additional charges. A notification in this regard was issued by the state home and general administration departments. As per the notification, Komal Meena has been appointed as rural superintendent of police (SP) in Patna. In another key posting, 2018-batch IPS officer Puran Kumar Jha, who was awaiting posting at Bihar police headquarters, has been posted as SP in Vigilance Investigation Bureau, Patna. He was transferred to police headquarters following the firing from an AK-47 rifle during Bihar Bandh in Siwan on July 25 over the alleged NEET paper leak protest. At that he was posted as Siwan SP. Aniket Kumar Dwivedi (2024-batch) has been transferred as SDPO-I, Jehanabad. Deepti Monali (IPS-2024) has been transferred from ASP Gaya to SDPO, Jamui. Hemant Singh (IPS-2024) has been transferred from ASP East Champaran to SDPO-I (Town), Bhagalpur. Karthikeyan A K (IPS-2024) has been posted as SDPO-II (Town), Muzaffarpur. Ketan Ashok Ingole (IPS-2024) has been posted as SDPO, Rajauli (Nawada). Prasanna Kumar M V (IPS-2024) has been transferred as SDPO, Narkatiaganj (West Champaran) and Saeem Raza (IPS-2024) has been posted as SDPO, Naugachhia. The govt has also made changes involving three IAS officers. Naveen Kumar, a 2011-batch IAS officer, currently serving as special secretary in prohibition, excise and registration department, will now also hold additional charge as managing director of Biada. He already holds additional charge as principal/secretary-level head of information and public relations department (IPRD) and MD of Bihar State Beverages Corporation, as specified in the notification. Industry department secretary Kundan Kumar has been relieved of the additional charge of MD, Biada. Vivek Ranjan Maitrey, a 2017-batch IAS officer transferred from the post of additional secretary in IPRD, has been appointed director of sports. Another 2017-batch officer, Anil Kumar, has been transferred from his position as director, IPRD, and appointed MD of Bihar State Building Construction Corporation Limited. He will also continue to hold additional charge as MD of Bihar State Samvad Samiti. Abhishek Palasiya, a 2020-batch IAS officer serving as joint secretary in the road construction department, has been appointed MD of Bihar State Educational Infrastructure Development Corporation Limited. Meanwhile, Shrikant Kundalik Khandekar, joint secretary in CMâs secretariat, has been given additional charge of joint secretary in industry department until further orders. The home department also transferred three BPS officers. Kundan Kumar (BPS-2007) has been transferred as SP (administration), Patna. Sonu Kumar Rai (BPS-2010) has been posted as SP (Rural), Vaishali and Dilip Kumar (BPS-2022) has been posted as SDPO, Triveniganj, Supaul. Previous order transferring Pankaj Kumar Singh to SDPO Triveniganj was cancelled. title: Centre appoints two directors, joint director to NTA amid NEET exam controversies and reforms
text: The Centre has appointed three senior officials, including two directors and a joint director, to the National Testing Agency (NTA) amid scrutiny over examination-related controversies. The appointments come as the government moves to strengthen the agencyâs functioning through structural reforms, including tighter paper evaluation, specialist involvement and changes to its examination management system. New Delhi : The Centre has appointed two directors and a joint director to the National Testing Agency (NTA), which has been facing flak for issues related to the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) paper leak, among other concerns. Ravi Kumar Singh (Indian Police Service officer) and Prasanna Venkatesh V, an Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer, have been appointed as directors in the NTA, according to separate orders dated August 27, issued by the personnel ministry. Amit Samdariya, a 2016 batch Indian Revenue Service (Customs and Indirect Taxes) officer, has been selected for appointment as joint director in the NTA, an order issued by the personnel ministry said. All three orders referenced a circular from the personnel ministry stating that the appointed officers must assume their new positions within three weeks of the orders' issuance, "failing which the process of debarment from the Central Staffing Scheme shall be initiated." Recently, the government announced a comprehensive overhaul of the examination system at the NTA, including implementing a four-tier paper checking process, removing 600 experts, and onboarding domain specialists, among other changes. title: 'Massive negligence': CJP's Ashutosh Ranka on NEET-PG disruption at Jaipur centre
text: Ranka also alleged that political attention was being diverted towards confrontations instead of school infrastructure. JAIPUR: The NEET-PG 2026 examination at the ION Digital Zone Sitapura centre in Jaipur was disrupted on Sunday due to an internal power supply issue, forcing authorities to postpone the test for candidates allotted to the centre. The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare said the examination for 2,445 candidates affected by the technical disruption has been rescheduled for September 5. The disruption triggered protests by candidates at the Sitapura centre, with some demanding cancellation of the examination nationwide. Watch NEET Paper Leak Traced To Contracted Paper Setters, Charge Sheet Likely This Month | Watch Reacting to the incident, Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) Co-Convener Ashutosh Ranka alleged that the disruption reflected "massive negligence" and questioned the preparedness of examination authorities. He also claimed that a similar issue had occurred during the All India AYUSH Post Graduate Entrance Test (AIAPGET) around 10 days ago. "I feel that just as the Rajasthan government banned our entry after realising the reality of the schools, they should now ban entry to all exam centres across Rajasthan. That way, the technical problems will be solved," he said. Calling the incident a serious lapse, Ranka said, "It is indeed massive negligence. In Rajasthan. Especially since the same problem occurred during the AYUSH PG exam just ten days ago, and now the same issue has arisen with the NEET PG exam." Ranka also criticised the Rajasthan government's handling of issues related to government schools and alleged that the focus was being shifted towards political confrontations instead of addressing structural problems in the education system. "So, you don't believe in solving structural problems. You channel all your energy into physical altercations, inciting violence, and filing FIRs. So, how will these problems be solved?" he said. "Problems will only be solved when the country's students take to the streets and protest against them. Because their focus is solely on concealing the truth. They aren't interested in fixing structural problems," Ranka added. Ranka further alleged that attention was being diverted from issues related to school infrastructure. "But what are you actually doing? You are inciting violence and sending goons; that is where you are focusing your energy. You simply do not care about the situation of the schools," he said.
